Munich on foot

The must-sees

  • Alte Pinakothek

    Museum · 1836

    Leo von Klenze’s gallery opened in 1836, one of the oldest public art museums. After bombing it was rebuilt with plain brick patches left visible, and it holds works by Dürer and Rubens.

    Look for: Find Dürer’s self-portrait of 1500. He paints himself facing straight out, long-haired, in a pose that recalls images of Christ.

  • Deutsches Museum

    Museum · 1925

    Engineer Oskar von Miller founded it in 1903, and the building on the island opened in 1925. It holds aircraft, ships and mine galleries among countless machines.

  • English Garden

    Park · 1789

    It was laid out from 1789 at the suggestion of Benjamin Thompson, later Count Rumford, as a park open to everyone. The fast Eisbach stream runs through it.

    Look for: Find the Chinese Tower, a five-storey wooden pagoda in the middle of a large beer garden.

  • Frauenkirche

    Church · 1488

    Built in only about twenty years and finished in 1488, the domes on the towers were added in 1525. A dark footprint in the entrance hall is known as the Devil’s Step.

    Look for: Inside, find the black marble tomb monument of Emperor Louis the Bavarian, who died in 1347.

  • Hofbräuhaus

    Venue · 1589

    Duke Wilhelm V founded the court brewery in 1589; the present hall dates from the 1890s. In 1920 the Nazi party announced its programme at a meeting in the hall upstairs.

    Look for: Along the walls, find the locked cabinets where regulars keep their own stone beer mugs.

  • Marienplatz

    Square

    Munich’s main square since the city’s founding in 1158, it was once the market and tournament ground. The Marian column was raised in 1638, during the Thirty Years’ War.

    Look for: On the column’s base, four armoured cherubs fight a lion, a dragon, a basilisk and a serpent, standing for war, hunger, plague and heresy.

  • Munich Residenz

    Palace

    The Wittelsbach dukes, electors and kings lived here from the late 1300s until 1918. Heavily bombed in the war, it was rebuilt and now holds the Treasury and the Antiquarium hall.

    Look for: At the gates on Residenzstraße, bronze lions hold shields. Passers-by rub the small lion faces on the shields for luck, which is why they shine.

  • New Town Hall

    Civic building · 1908

    Built in stages between 1867 and 1908 to designs by Georg von Hauberrisser. The Glockenspiel figures re-enact a royal wedding of 1568 and the coopers’ dance.

    Look for: At the very top of the tower stands the Münchner Kindl, the small hooded figure that is the city’s emblem.

  • Nymphenburg Palace

    Palace

    Elector Ferdinand Maria began it in 1664 for his wife after the birth of their heir. King Ludwig II was born here in 1845.

    Look for: Find the Gallery of Beauties: 36 portraits of women King Ludwig I admired, from princesses to a shoemaker’s daughter.

  • Olympic Park

    Park · 1972

    Günter Behnisch and Frei Otto designed the transparent tent roofs for the 1972 Games. Eleven members of the Israeli team were killed in a terrorist attack during the Olympics; a memorial in the park remembers them.

    Look for: Climb the Olympic Hill for a view down over the tent roofs, the lake and the tower.

  • Theresienwiese

    Venue · 1810

    It is named after Princess Therese, whose wedding to Crown Prince Ludwig in October 1810 was celebrated here with a horse race. The celebration became the Oktoberfest.

    Look for: On the slope at the western edge stands the bronze Bavaria with her lion. Stairs inside lead up into her head.

  • Viktualienmarkt

    Market · 1807

    The food market moved here from Marienplatz in 1807, when it had outgrown the square. Fountains among the stalls honour Munich’s folk singers and comedians, including Karl Valentin.

    Look for: Follow the maypole up: the painted figures fixed along it show the city’s trades and crafts.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Munich and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Munich passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
